first.rationale: Two of the three current pressures (onboarding completion down 4%, activation down 6%) are self-inflicted funnel issues with prior durable evidence of fixes (memory_31: signup simplification lifted SMB activation; memory_86: shortened onboarding lifted completion and time-to-value). Promotional pricing (memory_73) directly targets the competitor threat but risks attracting low-quality, price-sensitive accounts that could erode 'sustainable long-term qualified revenue'—the stated objective—so it's deprioritized for this single slot despite urgency. I verify memory_31 and memory_86 because they're the most directly overlapping with the current metric declines and because prior 'lift in activation/completion' findings need checking for whether they controlled for lead quality/downstream revenue, not just top-of-funnel rates, since a completion-rate lift achieved by trimming qualification-relevant fields could quietly degrade qualified revenue even while activation numbers look better. Given verification budget constraints, referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist are set aside since they don't address either the acute regressions or the competitive pressure this week. I'm treating this as a standard (not broad) experiment because we're intervening on a live regression with an inherited-but-unverified causal claim, and I want to preserve optionality if the archived record reveals the completion-rate gains came with a quality tradeoff.

mid.rationale: Verification confirms both records: exp_31 (signup simplification) shows signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%, but a small -1% dip in 30-day retention, and the conclusion explicitly notes it holds only for SMB, not replicated elsewhere. exp_86 (shortened onboarding) shows completion +13%, time-to-value improved, and retention +3%, a cleaner positive signal with no noted revenue tradeoff. Given this cycle's actual regressions are in onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and the competitor pricing threat is specifically hitting price-sensitive SMB accounts, a combined onboarding-simplification action targeted at SMB is the best single-slot bet for defending qualified revenue without directly engaging in a pricing race that risks attracting the same low-quality segment the competitor is targeting. I flag downstream_value_risk because exp_31's retention dip, even though small and offset by revenue gains, means we should track cohort quality (not just completion/activation) post-launch, especially since simplification could ease in lower-intent SMB signups right when a competitor is siphoning exactly that population. I keep this as a standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout because exp_31's conclusion explicitly limits confirmed effects to SMB and warns against generalizing, so scope should stay bounded to SMB accounts and be evaluated on qualified revenue and 30-day retention, not just top-of-funnel completion, before any wider rollout. Promotional pricing remains tabled this cycle: it directly answers the competitive threat but the memory record for it wasn't part of this verification, so I'm not increasing confidence in it, and reacting to competitor pricing with our own price cuts risks a race that erodes long-term qualified revenue, which is explicitly the objective we're optimizing for.

final2.rationale: The situation has materially changed since I committed to simplify_onboarding: a second, deeper competitor price cut plus doubled churn conversations among price-sensitive SMB accounts is now an acute retention threat, not just a slower-moving activation/completion problem. Onboarding simplification (exp_31/exp_86) addresses top-of-funnel adoption but does nothing to stop active SMB accounts from churning to a cheaper competitor this week, so it no longer matches the most urgent risk to qualified revenue. memory_73 (targeted promotional pricing for price-sensitive SMB, strong acquisition and revenue lift) is the directly relevant precedent for this threat, but I have not verified its archived source record this cycle and my budget is spent, so I'm treating it as inherited-but-unverified and deliberately keeping scale small. I'm switching the week's single experiment slot to a small_guarded_test of targeted promotional pricing aimed narrowly at the price-sensitive SMB accounts currently in churn conversations, rather than a broad rollout, because racing a competitor's pricing down risks exactly the kind of low-quality, margin-eroding revenue that conflicts with the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue — memory_73's own framing is about acquisition/revenue lift, not explicitly about defending retention under competitive duress, so I don't want to over-extend on an unverified analogy. downstream_value_risk_flagged is true because discounting to retain price-sensitive accounts can select for lower-LTV, low-loyalty customers and could need to be unwound later; this should be evaluated on qualified revenue and retention quality, not just short-term churn-prevention counts, before any wider commitment. I'm setting aside simplify_onboarding this week (its gains are real per verification but slower-acting and not competitive-threat-responsive), and continue to exclude referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist since neither addresses the immediate SMB pricing pressure leadership is asking about today.
